search_queries: "I wish Claude could" OR "is there an MCP for" reddit 2026
people complain AI assistant can't reliably do unit conversion timezone date math
found: The first query mostly surfaced existing Reddit-integration MCP servers, not a fresh gap. The second turned up a genuine, well-documented recurring problem: language models are unreliable at date/time arithmetic -- DST transitions, month/year rollover, and cross-timezone 'same time' scheduling -- because they compute it by approximate reasoning instead of calculation. A 2025 University of Edinburgh study (DateTimeReasoning) found even strong models fail basic clock/calendar questions, and developer write-ups describe silently-wrong UTC conversions in production agents.
why: Keyless (stdlib zoneinfo carries the full IANA tz database, no API or account needed), squarely inside 'gap in what Claude can do' (this is a case where a model should call a tool instead of reasoning it out), and checkable -- the fix is a deterministic function with a right answer, not a claim to trust.

built.description: An MCP server (stdio) wrapping five deterministic date/time functions: convert_timezone, add_time_delta, time_difference, date_facts, search_timezones.

works: 13 unit tests targeting the exact failure modes (spring-forward gap, fall-back fold, leap-day/month-end clamping, cross-timezone diff) all pass. Beyond unit tests: a real MCP client session connected over stdio, called list_tools and five live tool calls, and got correct answers -- e.g. 01:30 America/New_York + 1 hour on the 2026-03-08 spring-forward night correctly lands at 03:30 (02:30 doesn't exist that night), and 9am Los Angeles vs 9am Berlin on the same date comes back as 9 hours apart, not zero. Full transcript: tools/time-arithmetic/proof/run_2026-09-13.txt. Note: the first version of add_time_delta got the spring-forward case wrong on the first test run (it added the hour using the fixed UTC offset already attached to the datetime instead of going through UTC first) -- the test caught it before it shipped, which is itself a small piece of evidence for why deterministic, tested tools beat unverified reasoning here.

found: Three real, sharply-documented candidates surfaced: (1) word/character/token counting -- a genuine complaint (github.com/orgs/community/discussions/177647, multiple explainer posts on why LLMs can't count) but already covered by numerous existing MCP servers (text-count-mcp-server, mcp-wordcounter, and several more found on Glama/mcp.so). (2) Precise text diffing -- also real (AI document-comparison writeups explicitly note LLMs 'cannot replace the precision of a deterministic diff') but likewise already saturated with existing MCP diff/text-tools servers. (3) LLM randomness bias, the 'random number between 1 and 50 -> always 27' phenomenon: arxiv.org/html/2601.05414 ('LLMs Struggle to Generate Random Numbers from Statistical Distributions'), news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43823899, and springboards.ai/blog-posts/you-cant-ask-an-llm-to-be-more-random all document that models predict a plausible-looking 'random' answer from training-data frequency rather than sampling one -- a genuine 'call a tool instead of reasoning it out' gap. Randomness-generation MCP servers exist elsewhere too, but none found combine general-purpose CSPRNG utilities with a built-in, checkable proof of unbiasedness.
why: Picked LLM randomness over word-counting and text-diff: those two are real needs but the bar in TASKS.md is worth-to-feasibility, and worth is undercut when a need is already thoroughly served (word-count and diff both have many mature existing MCP servers) with no differentiated angle available. The randomness gap is just as sharply documented (the '27' finding is specific, repeated across independent write-ups, and reproduces across multiple vendors' assistants) and this repo's version has a real differentiator: verify_uniformity, a from-scratch chi-square goodness-of-fit test (no scipy needed) that turns 'this tool's output isn't biased' from a claim into a number you can check per range and sample size -- directly answering the documented failure mode rather than just providing another random-number tool.

built.description: An MCP server (stdio) wrapping ten CSPRNG-backed functions (secrets module, not random's Mersenne Twister): roll_dice, random_integers, random_floats, flip_coins, shuffle_list, pick_random, generate_password, generate_token, generate_uuid4, and verify_uniformity -- a chi-square uniformity test with a hand-rolled regularized-incomplete-gamma implementation, run and checked against textbook chi-square critical values.

works: 34 unit tests pass, including the chi-square p-value function checked against six textbook critical-value table entries, and a synthetic 'one bucket takes 90% of 10000 draws' histogram confirming the test actually flags bias (p < 1e-10) rather than only ever passing real randomness. Beyond unit tests: a real MCP client session over stdio called list_tools and all ten tools live, including running verify_uniformity on the exact range from the documented failure (1 to 50, 20000 draws) -- came back uniform (p around 0.3-0.85 across repeated runs, most-sampled value nowhere near a fixed '27', each value's observed share within ~0.2 percentage points of the 2% expected share). Full transcript: tools/secure-random/proof/run_2026-09-14.txt. Note: the first live-session pass surfaced a real bug, not just a proof-script issue -- shuffle_list/pick_random's untyped `list` return type made the MCP SDK skip structured-output generation and split the result across one text content block per element (silently losing type fidelity, e.g. ints came back as strings); annotating both as `list[Any]` fixed it, verified by re-running the live session before shipping.

why: No new-tool candidate cleared the worth-to-feasibility bar this cycle -- every candidate researched was already thoroughly served elsewhere in the MCP ecosystem, the same outcome as the previous cycle's search. built.description: 1) .github/workflows/test.yml: runs `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` for every tools/*/tests/ directory plus a collection-index sanity check, on pull_request and push:main, with a job named `test` matching auto-merge.yml's existing /deploy|build|test/i filter. 2) auto-merge.yml: added a 60-second grace period before concluding 'no relevant check exists' means 'nothing to wait for', closing a pull_request_target vs. pull_request event race. 3) tools/secure-random/randkit.py: pick_random gained an optional `weights` list (proportional-probability selection via a CSPRNG-backed cumulative-sum draw, both unique and with-replacement); a new _chi_square_fit generalizes the existing uniform-only chi-square code to arbitrary expected distributions; a new verify_weighted_distribution tool runs that generalized test against real weighted draws. server.py and manifest.json updated to expose both.

works: CI: both workflow YAML files parse and validate; ran the full local test suite (13 time-arithmetic + 47 secure-random + 4 collection-index = 64 tests, all green) before wiring test.yml to run the same commands in CI, so the new workflow matches what was actually verified. secure-random: 13 new unit tests (47 total, up from 34) covering weighted pick_random (favors the heavy item over 500 trials, never returns a zero-weight item over 200 trials, unique mode has no repeats, rejects mismatched-length/negative/all-zero weights) and verify_weighted_distribution (the _chi_square_fit generalization checked against a hand-built expected distribution; input validation). Live MCP client session over stdio (tools/secure-random/proof/run_2026-09-15.txt): weighted pick_random in both unique and with-replacement modes, unweighted pick_random confirmed unchanged, and verify_weighted_distribution run on weights [1,2,7] over 60,000 real CSPRNG draws landing within 0.3 percentage points of the requested 10%/20%/70% split (p ~ 0.13, chi2 = 4.14, df = 2) -- the same proof-not-assertion pattern verify_uniformity already established, now checkable for arbitrary weights too.

Discrete probability was different: a real, sharply-documented, and *recent* failure mode -- a 2026 paper on counterintuitive discrete-probability problems (arxiv.org/pdf/2606.07516) found models average 0.96 accuracy on standard probability problems but only 0.59 on counterintuitive ones, and the standalone 'LLMs Can't Do Probability' writeup (brainsteam.co.uk, also an active Hacker News discussion) documents the same failure informally. Existing calculator-style MCP servers (calculator-mcp-server, Math-MCP, SageMath-MCP) expose raw combinatorics primitives (nCr, nPr, factorial) but none found combine pre-composed word-problem scenarios (birthday paradox, Monty Hall, hypergeometric card odds) with a built-in Monte Carlo cross-check of the answer -- a genuinely open, differentiated angle.
why: Picked discrete-probability over declining every candidate again (which rule 9 would otherwise have triggered a third cycle running): the need is real, recent (2026 paper, not just older folklore), and specific -- counterintuitive probability, not generic arithmetic -- and this repo's differentiator (verify=true actually plays the scenario out via the same secrets-CSPRNG pattern tools/secure-random established, and checks the exact fraction against a Wilson confidence interval on the simulated frequency) is not something any server found in search does. It also builds on the existing collection rather than duplicating it, per TASKS.md's 'the collection should increasingly build on itself': the simulation machinery deliberately mirrors secure-random's proof-not-assertion approach and reuses the same CSPRNG source.

built.description: An MCP server (stdio) wrapping six exact discrete-probability functions -- birthday_collision, dice_sum_distribution, hypergeometric_probability, binomial_probability, bayes_update, monty_hall (a generalized N-door/N-car/N-reveal version, not just the classic 3-door case) -- each computed exactly via fractions.Fraction/math.comb, and each accepting verify=true to run a real CSPRNG Monte Carlo simulation of the scenario and report whether the exact answer falls inside a 95% Wilson confidence interval on the observed frequency.

works: 41 unit tests pass, including known textbook values (birthday-23/365 ~= 50.73%, classic Monty Hall 1/3 vs 2/3, 2d6 summing to 7 = 1/6, >=2 aces in a 5-card hand ~= 4.17%), full input validation, a cross-check where bayes_update's general Bayes'-theorem machinery and monty_hall's independently-derived closed-form formula are fed equivalent problems and land on the exact same fraction (2/3) via two unrelated code paths, and a 'does the check have teeth' test proving the Wilson-interval logic actually flags a wrong claim (not just passes a correct one) the same way secure-random's chi-square test does for bias. Beyond unit tests: a live MCP client session over stdio (tools/discrete-probability/proof/run_2026-09-16.txt) called list_tools and all six tools for real, several with verify=true showing the Monte Carlo frequency land next to the exact fraction across 30,000 real CSPRNG trials each (e.g. birthday_collision(23, 365): exact 0.507297 vs. simulated 0.510367, inside the 95% interval), plus confirmation that an invalid input (reveal count too large for the door/car count in a generalized Monty Hall) comes back as an MCP error result instead of a silently wrong number.

found: Ran collection-index first per the loop (4 tools, nothing to extend that clearly beat a fresh candidate). Per the previous cycle's notes-for-owner warning that 'single deterministic calculation' MCP ideas are actively saturated (pipeworx-io and others), this cycle deliberately searched for a different problem shape. General 'wish Claude could' and unit-conversion searches were unproductive (mostly SEO content / no sharp complaint). Two strong candidates surfaced: (1) NP-hard combinatorial optimization (knapsack/bin-packing/scheduling) -- real, well-documented failure (EHOP benchmark, 'A Knapsack by Any Other Name' ACL paper, several others show LLM end-to-end solving degrades sharply with instance scale) but already served by at least two existing MCP servers built on Google OR-Tools (MCP Optimizer, Opti-MCP), and OR-Tools is a heavy non-keyless-feeling dependency (large native binary) that cuts against this collection's stdlib-only discipline. (2) Logic grid ('zebra') puzzles -- also real and sharply documented: research on GPT-4o and grid logic puzzles found success rates as low as 8%, distinct from generic 'LLMs are bad at math' because the specific failure is iterative cross-checking of many simultaneous constraints, not arithmetic. Existing general constraint-solver MCP servers were found (z3-solver-mcp-server, mcp-solver, exposing SAT/SMT/ASP), but a separate line of research ('LLM-as-formalizer consistently underperforms LLM-as-solver' on real-life constraint problems) shows models are specifically bad at translating a puzzle into SMT-LIB/ASP in the first place -- so those tools' own precondition is itself a documented failure mode. Follow-up search for an MCP server exposing a logic-grid-puzzle-specific solver with a simple structured clue vocabulary (the same_house/next_to/left_of shape a few non-MCP web solvers like CacheSleuth's Logical Solver and zebra4j already use) found none.
why: Picked logic-grid-solver over the optimization-solver candidate: both are real, differentiated, and feasible, but optimization's existing MCP coverage (two servers, both on OR-Tools) is more direct competition than logic-grid-solver's (general SMT/ASP solvers that don't share its structured-clue angle at all), and OR-Tools' native-binary dependency sits awkwardly against 'keyless, credential-free, stdlib-only where possible' even though it doesn't need an API key. Logic-grid-solver also let this cycle extend the collection's established 'proof, not assertion' discipline (secure-random's chi-square tests, discrete-probability's Monte Carlo cross-checks) in a new way that fits a CSP domain specifically: prove the *puzzle* is well-posed (exactly one solution, not just *a* solution) by continuing the search for a second one, and independently re-verify any proposed grid against the clues via a separate code path rather than trusting the solver's own say-so.

built.description: An MCP server (stdio) exposing describe_clue_types, solve_logic_grid, and verify_logic_grid_solution. puzzlekit.py implements a small fixed clue vocabulary (position, same_position, different_position, immediately_left_of, immediately_right_of, left_of, right_of, next_to, not_next_to, distance) and solves puzzles via constraint propagation (arc consistency between every clue and each category's bijection-to-positions constraint, iterated to a fixpoint, with MRV backtracking whenever propagation alone doesn't finish) -- the standard technique real zebra-puzzle solvers use, not brute-force search. solve_logic_grid proves uniqueness by default by continuing the search for a second, distinct solution; verify_solution independently re-derives every clue's truth value by scanning a candidate grid fresh, a different code path from the solver's own internal search state, and is exposed standalone so any proposed answer (the solver's own, or a hand-written guess) can be checked on its own.

works: 28 unit tests (tests/test_puzzlekit.py): the classic 5-house Einstein zebra puzzle solved end-to-end and checked against its published answer (the German owns the zebra, the Norwegian drinks water), its uniqueness proven, all 15 of its clues independently re-verified; every one of the 10 clue types exercised on a small hand-checkable 3-position puzzle; contradictory clues raising instead of returning a wrong answer; an under-constrained puzzle correctly reported as *not* unique with a concrete alternate solution returned; the verifier catching a deliberately wrong guess and structurally malformed grids (duplicate/missing items, out-of-range position keys) instead of rubber-stamping them; input validation for every malformed-input path; and a max_nodes budget cap that fails predictably instead of hanging. Live MCP client session over stdio (tools/logic-grid-solver/proof/run_2026-09-17.txt): list_tools, describe_clue_types, the classic zebra puzzle solved in 5 search nodes and proven unique, its own solution independently re-verified clue-by-clue, a deliberately wrong guess (two houses' assignments swapped) caught by the verifier (all_satisfied: false, the specific violated clue flagged), an under-constrained puzzle correctly reported as unique: false with its alternate solution shown, and contradictory clues (the same item placed at two positions) coming back as an MCP tool error rather than a silently wrong answer. Caught and fixed a real bug before shipping, not after: the first backtracking implementation (position-then-category assignment order with incremental constraint checking) had a dependency-counter bug -- on backtrack it only restored the counter for clues that had become fully checked, not every clue touched by the assignment, so a later branch could evaluate a clue against a position that had since been unassigned, crashing with a KeyError. Caught immediately by the test suite (not by the live session) on the very first run; fixed, and separately, the initial naive backtracking search (correct but with only incremental-checking pruning) took over 25 seconds and still didn't finish the classic 5x5 zebra puzzle within a 3,000,000-node budget, so it was replaced with the constraint-propagation approach described above, which solves the same puzzle in 5 nodes and under 2ms.

found: Ran collection-index first per the loop (5 tools, nothing to extend that clearly beat a fresh candidate this cycle). Per the standing guidance in notes-for-owner.md (the 'single deterministic calculation' shape is actively saturated, and even the 'different problem shape' move that produced logic-grid-solver should not just be repeated as another constraint-satisfaction puzzle), this cycle deliberately searched for a problem shape neither calculation nor static constraint satisfaction. Sudoku surfaced early as a documented LLM failure (Univ. of Colorado Boulder study: none of GPT/Gemini/DeepSeek solved even 6x6 puzzles reliably, can't backtrack once wrong) but was rejected as too close to logic-grid-solver's own shape (constraint satisfaction over a static grid) and separately heavily saturated by non-MCP sudoku solvers. Planning -- finding a sequence of state-changing actions to reach a goal -- surfaced as a genuinely different shape: Kambhampati et al.'s PlanBench/Blocksworld research is extensive and sharply documented (LLMs, even with chain-of-thought, fail reliably past a handful of objects because a valid plan requires tracking cumulative state across interdependent actions and backtracking when an early choice blocks a later goal -- a search problem, not a language one). Checked for existing MCP coverage: found exactly one general planning MCP server (byte4ever/gp, a Go wrapper around Graphplan) that requires the caller to already speak PDDL or full ADL (disjunctive preconditions, conditional effects, quantifiers) -- no keyless MCP server was found exposing planning through a small fixed JSON vocabulary with an independent plan verifier. Also checked and rejected: round-robin tournament scheduling (real combinatorial-generation need, but every result was a plain non-MCP scheduling library/script, no sharply-documented 'LLMs get this wrong' failure mode behind it -- didn't clear the TASKS.md step 2 bar on its own) and cryptarithmetic/SEND+MORE=MONEY solving (real CSP shape but, like sudoku, overlaps logic-grid-solver's existing shape rather than opening a new one, and is already extremely well covered by non-MCP solvers).
why: Picked strips-planner over the sudoku and round-robin/cryptarithmetic candidates: planning is the only one of the three that is (a) sharply and extensively documented as a distinct LLM failure mode with its own research literature (PlanBench), not just an anecdote, (b) a genuinely different problem shape from every tool already in this collection -- sequential action search with cumulative, interdependent state, not a static constraint assignment (logic-grid-solver) or a single calculation (secure-random/discrete-probability/time-arithmetic) -- directly answering last cycle's own note-for-owner about not just repeating the CSP move, and (c) has a real but narrow gap in the existing MCP ecosystem: the one general planner found requires PDDL/ADL input, which research on 'LLM-as-formalizer' shows models are themselves unreliable at producing, so requiring it doesn't actually fix the problem for a calling model. Building a small-fixed-vocabulary planner (mirroring the exact move logic-grid-solver already made for its own puzzle shape) closes that gap without duplicating either the existing Go/PDDL server or logic-grid-solver's own CSP mechanics -- BFS state-space search with proof-of-optimality and proof-of-unsolvability is a different algorithm entirely from arc-consistency + backtracking.

built.description: An MCP server (stdio) exposing describe_planning_format, solve_planning_problem, verify_plan, and generate_blocks_world_problem. planner.py implements a small fixed JSON vocabulary for facts ([predicate, ...args]), action schemas (parameters/preconditions/add/delete, with 'not'-prefixed negated preconditions), and goals, grounds every action schema over the supplied objects, and solves via breadth-first search over the grounded state space -- which both proves the returned plan is the shortest possible (BFS explores fewer-action states first) and, when no plan exists, proves the goal is unreachable by exhausting the entire reachable state space rather than just giving up. A separate budget-exceeded path (max_states/max_depth) raises instead of claiming either proof when the search is genuinely inconclusive. verify_plan is a deliberately separate, simpler forward-simulation code path that independently replays any candidate plan one action at a time and reports exactly which step and which unmet precondition breaks it. generate_blocks_world_problem builds a random, reproducible (seeded) instance of the classic Blocksworld benchmark domain the LLM-planning-failure literature uses.

works: 25 unit tests (tests/test_planner.py): a light-switch toy domain including a negated-goal case; the classic Sussman anomaly (the canonical example showing naive 'achieve goals one at a time' planning fails) solved and checked against its known-optimal 6-action plan (unstack, putdown, pickup, stack, pickup, stack), with the solver's own plan independently re-verified via a separate verify_plan call; verify_plan catching an unmet precondition, a wrong argument count, an unknown action, an unknown object, and a plan whose steps all succeed but don't actually reach the goal; a contradictory goal (on(a,b) and on(b,a) simultaneously) correctly proven unreachable by exhausting the state space, versus a too-small search budget correctly raising instead of claiming that same proof; input validation for every malformed-input path; and the Blocksworld generator's reproducibility (identical instance for the same seed), its generated instances being solvable and independently verifiable across ten different seeds, and its num_blocks range validation. Live MCP client session over stdio (tools/strips-planner/proof/run_2026-09-18.txt): list_tools, describe_planning_format, the Sussman anomaly solved in 18 expanded states and independently re-verified, a deliberately broken plan (picking up a block still buried under another) caught by verify_plan with the exact unmet precondition named, a generated 5-block Blocksworld instance (seed 2026) solved and independently verified end to end, a provably unsolvable goal correctly reported as such (state space exhausted, not unsearched), and a too-small search budget correctly coming back as an MCP tool error (is_error: true) rather than a silent wrong answer. Also discovered and worked around, while building the live-session proof, that the installed mcp==2.2.0 package does not populate structuredContent/outputSchema for any tool in this server (nor, spot-checked, for logic-grid-solver's own tools under the same installed version) -- every tool's JSON comes back only in the text content block. Not a bug in this tool's code; noted in progress/notes-for-owner.md since it may affect how other tools' proof transcripts should be gathered on this mcp version.

why: Picked graph-algorithms over continuing to search the vaguer 'entity tracking/long-conversation-memory' angle or reopening combinatorial puzzle generation, for three reasons: (a) it is the most sharply and *currently* documented of the candidates -- four separate purpose-built benchmarks in 2025/2026 alone, not one anecdotal complaint; (b) it is a genuinely different problem shape from all six existing tools -- structural traversal/optimization over an explicit graph, where correctness depends on exact state (running distances, in-degrees, tree membership, residual capacities) staying consistent across the whole computation, distinct from sequential action search (strips-planner), constraint satisfaction over a static assignment (logic-grid-solver), and single-formula calculation (the other three) -- directly following the standing 'keep looking for genuinely different shapes' guidance in current.md; and (c) it has a real, checked-and-confirmed gap in the existing MCP ecosystem (mcp-solver's formalization requirement, GDS Agent's Neo4j requirement), so this isn't rebuilding something that already exists elsewhere -- and it's fully buildable and provable in one session with four classic, well-understood algorithms, unlike graph coloring (also documented, but NP-hard and needing its own backtracking/budget story -- explicitly deferred rather than built half-attentively, see this tool's own README and progress/notes-for-owner.md).

built.description: An MCP server (stdio) exposing describe_graph_format plus a solve+verify pair for each of four classic graph algorithms, all reading the same small fixed node/edge JSON vocabulary. shortest_path solves via Dijkstra's algorithm (weight >= 0, defaults to 1); verify_shortest_path independently recomputes via Bellman-Ford -- a structurally different algorithm -- and checks the formal shortest-path optimality conditions. topological_sort solves via Kahn's algorithm, returning a concrete cycle (found via DFS) as proof when the graph isn't a DAG rather than just reporting 'cyclic'; verify_topological_order independently checks the direct definition. minimum_spanning_tree solves via Kruskal's algorithm (union-find); verify_minimum_spanning_tree independently proves minimality via the cycle-property exchange argument -- the standard mathematical proof of MST optimality, not a second run of Kruskal's. max_flow solves via Edmonds-Karp and always returns a minimum cut alongside the flow, whose capacity equal to the flow value IS the optimality proof (max-flow min-cut theorem); verify_max_flow independently checks flow conservation and capacity constraints, and, given a cut, whether it proves optimality. generate_random_graph gives a seeded, reproducible random graph to experiment with.

works: 44 unit tests (tests/test_graphkit.py): a known-by-hand shortest path on a small directed weighted graph (cross-checked manually: A-C-B-D-E = 3+2+1+2 = 8, beating the direct A-B-D-E and A-C-D-E routes), directed-edges-cannot-be-used-backwards vs. undirected-allows-it, an unreachable target proven (not guessed) by exhausting Dijkstra's frontier, negative weights rejected, and verify_shortest_path independently catching a wrong distance claim and a path using a nonexistent edge; a diamond DAG's topological order matched exactly, a 3-node cycle's concrete witness extracted and checked edge-by-edge against the real edge set, a partial-cycle graph correctly still ordering its acyclic part, and verify_topological_order catching a backwards edge and a non-permutation order; a known-minimum spanning tree (hand-verified: AB+BC+CD = 1+2+3 = 6, skipping the heavier AC/AD edges) matched exactly, a disconnected graph correctly returned as a forest, and verify_minimum_spanning_tree catching a deliberately suboptimal tree via the cycle-property check (naming the exact violating edge), a cyclic claimed tree, an edge not present in the graph, and incomplete spanning; a known max flow value on a small textbook flow network (S-A-B-T, max flow 5) matched exactly with its min cut's capacity also equal to 5 (both proving each other optimal), flow conservation and capacity constraints checked directly on every edge, and verify_max_flow catching a capacity violation, a conservation violation, correctly reporting an under-flow as feasible-but-unproven-optimal without a cut, and correctly refusing to accept a mismatched cut as an optimality proof; the random graph generator's reproducibility (identical graph for the same seed) and its output composing cleanly into minimum_spanning_tree and shortest_path; and shared input validation (duplicate nodes, self-loops, unknown node references, non-numeric weights, duplicate flow edges, missing capacity, source == sink). Full repo test suite green locally: 202 tests across all seven tools (158 from before, plus graph-algorithms' 44). Live MCP client session over stdio driving the real server, not just scaffolding (tools/graph-algorithms/proof/run_2026-09-19.txt): list_tools, describe_graph_format, the known shortest path solved and independently verified, a deliberately wrong distance claim caught, the diamond DAG ordered and the 3-cycle's witness returned, the known MST found and the deliberately suboptimal one caught, the known max flow found with its matching min cut and a deliberately invalid flow assignment caught, a generated random graph fed straight into minimum_spanning_tree, and a negative edge weight correctly coming back as an MCP tool error (is_error: true) instead of a wrong or silent answer. python3 tools/collection-index/index.py and python3 scripts/build_site.py both pick up the new tool correctly.

built.description: Three new MCP tools added to the existing graph-algorithms server. graph_coloring finds a proper coloring using at most num_colors colors (labeled 0..num_colors-1) via backtracking search -- DSATUR variable ordering (always branch on the uncolored node with the most distinctly-colored neighbors) plus forward checking (a tentative color assignment removes that color from uncolored neighbors' domains; a domain emptying out prunes the branch immediately) -- capped by a max_search_nodes budget: exhausting the whole search tree without a colorable branch is returned as colorable: false with a proof, while running out of budget first raises instead of silently guessing 'not colorable', the same solved-vs-inconclusive contract strips-planner's max_states/max_depth already established. verify_coloring independently checks a claimed coloring against the direct definition (every node has exactly one color, no edge joins two same-colored nodes) -- no search at all, a structurally different and much simpler code path than the backtracking solver. chromatic_number finds the minimum number of colors a graph needs: a greedy clique gives a lower bound L for free (L pairwise-adjacent nodes each need a distinct color, so fewer than L colors can never work -- no search required for that half of the proof) and a greedy Welsh-Powell coloring gives a guaranteed-reachable upper bound; backtracking search then tries k = L, L+1, ... upward, so the chromatic number is the first colorable k, and every k ruled out along the way was proven uncolorable by a fully exhausted search, not merely unfound. All three tools always treat the graph as undirected and ignore weight/capacity, since only adjacency matters for coloring.

works: 17 new unit tests added to tests/test_graphkit.py (61 total for graph-algorithms, up from 44; 219 across all seven tools, up from 202): a triangle (K3) correctly colorable with 3 colors but proven uncolorable with 2 (not just unfound), a bipartite 4-cycle colored with 2, weight/directedness confirmed ignored, invalid num_colors/max_search_nodes rejected, and a deliberately too-small search budget raising ValueError instead of returning a wrong 'not colorable' answer; verify_coloring accepting a valid coloring, catching two adjacent nodes sharing a color (naming the exact edge), a missing node, an unexpected node, a bad color type, and accepting both integer and string color labels; chromatic_number correctly finding 3 for a triangle and 2 for a 4-cycle with the clique lower bound alone proving minimality (zero exhaustive search needed, k_values_proven_uncolorable == []), and -- the test that actually exercises the search machinery -- finding 3 for a 5-cycle (C5), which is triangle-free so its clique lower bound is only 2, meaning k=2 must be genuinely, exhaustively ruled out by real backtracking search before k=3 is found colorable; a single isolated node's chromatic number correctly 1; a budget-exceeded case raising; and a generated random graph's chromatic_number cross-checked end-to-end by confirming graph_coloring genuinely reports one fewer color as not colorable. Full repo test suite green locally: 219 tests across all seven tools. Live MCP client session over stdio driving the real server (tools/graph-algorithms/proof/run_2026-09-20.txt): list_tools showing all three new tools registered, the triangle colored with 3 and proven uncolorable with 2, verify_coloring catching two adjacent nodes sharing a color, the 5-cycle's chromatic number (3) computed with real search at k=2 first, a too-small max_search_nodes budget correctly coming back as an MCP tool error (is_error: true) instead of a silently wrong answer, a generated random graph fed straight into chromatic_number and cross-checked, and shortest_path (a pre-existing tool) confirmed still working unchanged alongside the new ones. python3 tools/collection-index/index.py and python3 scripts/build_site.py both pick up the updated tool correctly.
